title: SURE-RAG: Sufficiency and Uncertainty-Aware Evidence Verification for Selective Retrieval-Augmented Generation
research_question: Can a structured set-level verifier determine whether retrieved evidence is sufficient to support a candidate answer and use uncertainty-aware selective prediction to abstain when that support is inadequate?
methodology: SURE-RAG uses a shared DeBERTa-v3-base cross-encoder to produce support, refutation, and neutral relation distributions for claim-evidence pairs, then aggregates those local outputs into answer-level coverage, relation-strength, uncertainty, and retrieval feature blocks. A logistic-regression aggregator predicts Supported, Refuted, or Insufficient, and an uncertainty-penalized selective score determines whether the system answers or abstains; calibration parameters and thresholds are selected only from development data. The main HotpotQA-RAG v3 benchmark contains 4,026 examples in 900 question groups with full, partial, hard-insufficient, irrelevant, and refuting evidence conditions and group-disjoint splits. Evaluation includes classification F1, selective risk at fixed coverage, calibration error, shortcut diagnostics, counterfactual evidence swaps, a GPT-4o audit, no-oracle variants, HaluBench transfer, and ablations.

key_findings.finding: On controlled HotpotQA-RAG v3, calibrated SURE-RAG reaches 0.9075 Macro-F1 and raw SURE-RAG reaches 0.8951, substantially above DeBERTa mean-pooling at 0.6516 and comparable to the strong concat cross-encoder at 0.8888.

Set-level answer aggregation materially improves over pooling-only verification, supporting the paper's argument that evidence sufficiency cannot be reduced to selecting the individually most supportive passage.
SURE-RAG provides a strong low-coverage selective-ranking benefit, but this advantage does not constitute a strict high-coverage or anytime-valid risk guarantee.
key_findings.section: VI-D Selective Answering and VII-A Interpretation

key_findings.finding: Post-hoc calibration improves binary expected calibration error from 0.0304 to 0.0198 but does not improve Risk@30, which changes from 0.1642 to 0.1670.

Counterfactual swaps show near-perfect sensitivity to degradation of the evidence set on the controlled benchmark, including perfect reported success for partial, hard-insufficient, and irrelevant evidence substitutions.

External transfer exposes a sharp task boundary: SURE-RAG outperforms GPT-4o on the controlled HotpotQA-RAG v3 comparison, while GPT-4o strongly outperforms SURE-RAG for unsafe-answer detection on natural HaluBench.
key_findings.section: VI-G GPT-4o Judge and External Transfer

key_findings.finding: Removing retrieval-uncertainty features reduces Macro-F1 from 0.8951 for raw SURE-RAG to 0.8370, indicating that the retrieval-information block is important in this constructed benchmark.

limitations: The principal benchmark is a controlled QA-derived construction rather than naturally occurring RAG logs or free-form long-form generation.
The maximum shortcut-baseline artifact ratio is 0.6816, so the constructed benchmark retains moderate artifact risk.
Entity-swap refutation generation can introduce answer-type mismatches and label noise.
Experiments validate short-answer sufficiency rather than long-form multi-claim evidence completeness.
The method targets controlled evidence sufficiency and does not generalize well to open-world hallucination detection in the reported HaluBench transfer.
GPT-4o auditing supplements but does not replace large-scale human annotation.
The aggregator combines local claim-passage signals rather than performing end-to-end reasoning jointly across passages.
The selective score is empirically calibrated but does not furnish an anytime-valid or formal bounded-risk stopping guarantee.
Temporal validity, evidence-version identity, permission-aware access, and adaptive decisions about what evidence to retrieve next are outside the evaluated method.
The processed HotpotQA-RAG v3 files and evaluation artifacts are described as planned releases rather than already available artifacts in the paper.
raw_claims: SURE-RAG distinguishes supported, refuted, and insufficient evidence rather than treating retrieval relevance as sufficient grounding.
A shared cross-encoder scores each claim-evidence pair before answer-level aggregation.
The aggregator includes coverage, relation, uncertainty, and retrieval-derived feature blocks.
The system abstains unless its predicted class is Supported and its uncertainty-adjusted score clears a development-selected threshold.
HotpotQA-RAG v3 contains multiple evidence conditions derived from the same underlying questions and uses question-group-disjoint splits.
Calibrated SURE-RAG has the highest reported Macro-F1 among the main controlled-benchmark configurations.
Calibration lowers binary ECE but does not improve the reported Risk@30 value.
The counterfactual evidence experiment shows that supported probability falls reliably when full evidence is replaced by degraded evidence.
SURE-RAG transfers poorly to natural HaluBench unsafe-answer detection compared with GPT-4o.
Pooling-only and the variant without retrieval uncertainty both perform materially below the full raw system.
The authors characterize the current evidence as controlled-benchmark validation rather than a complete solution to open-world hallucination.
Release of processed benchmark files, split identifiers, predictions, configurations, and evaluation scripts is described as planned.
